newsitem.title: USA: Ex-detective in Simpson case charged with perjury.
newsitem.headline: Ex-detective in Simpson case charged with perjury.

text.p: Former Los Angeles police detective Mark Fuhrman was charged with perjury on Wednesday for testifying at the O.J. Simpson murder trial that he had not used a racial slur anytime in the past 10 years.
A conviction on the perjury charge could bring up to three years in prison.
Fuhrman, who retired from the police force last year and now lives in Idaho, pleaded not guilty to a single felony charge and was allowed to remain free on his own recognisance.
The criminal case against Fuhrman, a key investigator in the 1994 murders of Simpson's ex-wife and her friend, stemmed from a year-long investigation by the California attorney general's office.

Fuhrman is accused of lying on the witness stand on March 15, 1995, when he testified that "he had not addressed any black person as a 'nigger' or spoken about black people as 'niggers'" in the past decade, according to a criminal complaint.
After his testimony, an aspiring screenwriter brought to court taped interviews with Fuhrman in which he uttered the racial slur dozens of times and bragged about beating and torturing suspects.
When Fuhrman was called back to the witness stand, he invoked his constitutional right against self-incrimination and refused to answer most questions.

The defence team built its case around allegations that Fuhrman was a racist who planted the bloody glove found at Simpson's estate after the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. Simpson was acquitted last Oct. 3.

Fuhrman made his first appearance before a municipal judge in a high-security courtroom where reporters and spectators had to sit behind thick glass. His attorney, Darryl Mounger, entered a not-guilty plea on his client's behalf, and the judge ordered Fuhrman to an immediate pre-trial hearing in another courtroom.
There, only minutes later, Superior Court Judge James Bascue asked Fuhrman to again enter his plea. Fuhrman stood at the defence table and said firmly: "Not guilty."

The Los Angeles police department has been conducting an internal investigation that has so far failed to turn up any evidence that Fuhrman and other officers brutalized suspects as he claimed in the tape-recorded interviews, police sources said.

As Fuhrman walked out of the courtroom, a man shoved court papers into his hands and declared loudly: "Mark Fuhrman, you are served, buddy." It was believed to be a subpoena from Simpson's defence team ordering him to testify in the civil wrongful-death case brought by the victims' families.

Simpson's attorneys in his civil trial, which got under way last month in Santa Monica, want Fuhrman to take the witness stand again in hopes of bolstering the defence case. But it remained unclear whether Fuhrman could be forced to return to Los Angeles to testify.
